read.title: Three ways to attack a problem
text: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller copies of itself, solves them recursively, and combines the results. Merge sort is the model: split the array in half, sort each half, and merge them in linear time, for O(n log n) in every case. Because merging takes from the left half on ties, merge sort is stable. Quicksort also divides, around a pivot, and is fast on average, but a run of bad pivots pushes it to O(n²).

Dynamic programming applies when the same subproblems appear again and again and an optimal answer is built from optimal answers to smaller pieces. Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially many times; storing each result once, by memoizing top-down or tabulating bottom-up, makes it linear.

A greedy algorithm makes the choice that looks best right now and never reconsiders. That is fast, and for some problems, such as building a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm, it is provably optimal. For others it fails. Making change for 6 with coins of 1, 3, and 4, greedy grabs the 4 and ends with three coins, while two 3s would do. Before trusting greedy, prove that local choices cannot paint you into a corner.
